name: IO-Link
description: A standardized point-to-point communication protocol that digitizes the connection between simple industrial sensors/actuators and a controller, over the existing 3-wire cable.
how_it_works: Overlays digital communication on the standard 3-wire sensor cable (24V, GND, switching signal becomes a digital comms line), enabling parameterization and diagnostics alongside the process data.
use_cases: Smart industrial sensors/actuators with remote configuration/diagnostics
advantages: Uses standard, unshielded 3-wire sensor cabling
Enables remote parameterization/diagnostics of simple sensors
limitations: Point-to-point only (needs an IO-Link master to aggregate multiple sensors)
real_world_example: A proximity sensor on a production line reporting not just on/off but also temperature and duty-cycle diagnostics via IO-Link.
frame_note: IO-Link point-to-point uses a modified UART at 4.8 kbit/s with 24 V wake-up pulses; the checksum is a simple 8-bit sum protecting the unidirectional command sequence.

name: TLS / SSL

description: Transport Layer Security (successor to the original Netscape SSL) — the cryptographic protocol securing virtually all HTTPS web traffic.
how_it_works: A handshake negotiates cipher suites and exchanges keys (via asymmetric crypto), then symmetric encryption protects the actual data for speed.
advantages: Provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication
Continuously updated to counter new cryptographic attacks
limitations: Adds computational overhead — can be costly for very constrained MCUs (mitigated by TLS-PSK, DTLS)
real_world_example: The padlock icon in your browser indicating your connection to a website is TLS-encrypted.
frame_note: Every TLS record carries content type, version and length. TLS 1.3 hides the content type inside the ciphertext (outer byte reads 'application data') and protects the header itself as additional authenticated data.

name: WPA2 / WPA3
description: The security protocols protecting Wi-Fi networks from eavesdropping and unauthorized access.

frame_note: WPA3 replaces the TKIP MIC with an 8-byte GCM tag; SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) resists offline dictionary attacks on the PSK.

name: MACsec
description: Provides encryption and integrity protection at the Ethernet (Layer 2) level, securing traffic between directly connected switches/devices.

name: ARINC 429
organization: ARINC Industry Activities (the standards body was sold to SAE International in Jan 2014; Collins Aerospace bought the separate ARINC business)
description: The most widely used avionics data bus standard, defining how flight computers and instruments exchange data in most commercial aircraft.
how_it_works: Unidirectional, single-transmitter/multiple-receiver broadcast on a twisted pair, sending fixed 32-bit words at one of two speeds.
frame_note: ARINC 429 is bipolar return-to-zero: a 200 ns pulse at the start of each bit period carries the data, and the duty cycle (75 % / 25 % of the 100 or 12.5 kbit/s period) encodes the logical value. Odd parity is checked over the whole 32-bit label.
use_cases: Commercial aircraft avionics (flight computers, navigation instruments)
advantages: Extremely robust and deterministic — decades of proven reliability
Simple unidirectional broadcast simplifies certification/analysis
limitations: Low bandwidth by modern standards
Unidirectional — needs a separate bus per direction, increasing wiring
real_world_example: A Boeing 737's flight management computer broadcasting airspeed data to multiple cockpit instruments via ARINC 429.

technical.signaling: Unidirectional bipolar differential avionics bus.
technical.logic_high: Positive differential state, typically about +6.5 to +8 V.
technical.logic_low: Negative differential state, typically about −6.5 to −8 V.
technical.voltage_reference: Bipolar differential levels; exact thresholds and common mode are standard-defined.
technical.clocking: Self-clocked data at 12.5 or 100 kbit/s in common implementations.
technical.termination_and_biasing: Qualified characteristic impedance, termination, coax/twisted-pair wiring, and protection.
design_notes: ARINC 429 uses bipolar pulse widths; polarity carries the logic state.
technical.max_distance: ARINC 429: 100+ m twisted/shielded; qualified harness per airframe.
technical.max_nodes: ARINC 429: 1 transmitter + up to 20 receivers; redundant channels per criticality.
technical.duplex_mode: Simplex (ARINC 429) or redundant dual-channel; higher layers add duplex.
technical.addressing: Label/SDI addressing plus system integration tables.
technical.error_detection: Parity + CRC + voter/monitor logic; redundancy management detects babbling units.
technical.line_encoding: Bipolar RZ (ARINC 429), Manchester/differential per avionics standard.
technical.power_profile: 28 V aircraft power via qualified converters; hold-up and lightning margins required.
technical.emc_isolation: Shielded/qualified wiring, lightning (DO-160) + HIRF protection, isolation barriers.
transceivers: ARINC 429 line drivers: DDC DEI1016 family

name: ARINC 664 (AFDX)

use_cases: Modern aircraft avionics networks (Airbus A380, A350, Boeing 787)
advantages: Much higher bandwidth than ARINC 429
Deterministic guarantees despite using standard Ethernet hardware
limitations: More complex certification/configuration (Virtual Link bandwidth allocation)

frame_note: AFDX frames interleave on one link: the 8-bit preamble plus a minimum IFG lets a switch detect frame starts without carrier sense, and BAG sets the bandwidth allocation gap that bounds jitter.

name: JTAG (IEEE 1149.1)
description: The universal silicon debug and boundary-scan port — the 4/5-wire interface behind virtually every firmware flash, breakpoint, and factory board test since 1990.
how_it_works: A probe drives TCK/TMS while TDI/TDO form a shift chain through every TAP on the board. A 16-state TAP controller selects the Instruction Register, then shifts Data Registers (IDCODE, BYPASS, BOUNDARY) to flash, halt, inspect, or boundary-scan the silicon.
speed: TCK 1–50 MHz typical (up to ~100 MHz on short chains)
use_cases: Factory boundary-scan board testing (no test firmware needed)
advantages: One port flashes, debugs, and production-tests the board
Daisy-chains across every chip with no extra pins per device
limitations: 4-5 wires plus a probe — costly on tiny boards
Slow compared to SWD for Cortex-M; long chains divide TCK
real_world_example: An ST-Link or J-Link flashing an STM32 and halting it on a breakpoint over the 20-pin Cortex debug header.
fun_fact: JTAG was designed for testing boards, not debugging chips — the Joint Test Action Group only wanted a way to check solder joints. Chip vendors then smuggled entire debug architectures (ARM CoreSight, RISC-V DTM) through the same 4 wires.
fun_fact_source: IEEE Std 1149.1-2013 scope and history (boundary-scan test); ARM CoreSight architecture (debug reuse of the TAP).
frame_note: This protocol has no fixed bit-level frame of its own: its data is carried by the physical/link layer below it, or it is a method inside a higher-layer message format. See the Electrical & Hardware Profile for the carrier that frames it.

name: CAN XL
description: The third CAN generation: classic arbitration plus a 10+ Mbps data phase and up to 2048-byte payloads, aimed at software-defined vehicles and Ethernet tunneling.
how_it_works: Arbitration runs at Classic-CAN speed, then the bus switches to a fast data phase (separate transceiver mode) carrying up to 2048 bytes with 32-bit CRCs — fast enough to tunnel 100BASE-T1 Ethernet frames.
speed: 500 kbps – 1 Mbps arbitration; 2–20 Mbps data phase; 2048-byte payload
use_cases: Tunneling Ethernet/IP traffic over CAN wiring
advantages: ~30x the payload of CAN FD on familiar 2-wire buses
Ethernet interoperability without new wiring
limitations: Needs CAN XL SIC transceivers everywhere — no mixed classic-CAN segments
Ecosystem (controllers, tools) still ramping
real_world_example: A zonal gateway tunneling camera-configuration Ethernet traffic across the legacy CAN harness using CAN XL.
frame_note: CAN XL uses in-frame multiplexing for addressing up to 1024 nodes and payload segments up to 2048 bytes, trading classic CAN arbitration for throughput.

name: ISO-TP (ISO 15765-2)
description: The segmentation layer that lets a 4 KB UDS diagnostic message ride on 8-byte CAN frames — Single, First, Consecutive and Flow-Control frames with sequence numbers.
how_it_works: Payloads of 7 bytes or less go in one Single Frame; longer ones open with a First Frame announcing total length, stream Consecutive Frames (4-bit sequence numbers), and pause for Flow-Control frames that set block size and separation time.
speed: Bound by the carrier CAN/CAN FD bus (no speed of its own)
frame_note: N_PCI is 1 byte for Single/Consecutive frames, 2+ bytes for First/Flow frames. Payload caps at 4095 bytes total, 62 bytes per CAN FD frame.
use_cases: UDS fault-memory reads and ECU reflashing
Any diagnostic transfer bigger than one CAN frame
advantages: Makes big diagnostics work on small frames with flow control
Standardized addressing (normal/extended/mixed) across OEMs
limitations: Half-duplex stop-and-wait per block — throughput far below bus rate
Wrong STmin/blocksize settings stall or flood the ECU
real_world_example: A dealer tool reading a 2 KB freeze-frame buffer from an engine ECU via UDS-over-ISO-TP at 500 kbps CAN.

name: SOME/IP
description: Scalable service-Oriented MiddlewarE over IP — how software-defined vehicles discover services and call methods, subscribe to events, and push fields over Automotive Ethernet.
how_it_works: Services are discovered via SOME/IP-SD multicast; then methods (RPC), events (pub/sub) and fields (notifier/getter/setter) ride on UDP or TCP with a compact header carrying message/service/method IDs.
speed: 100 Mbps – 10 Gbps (bound by the Ethernet link, not the middleware)
advantages: True service orientation with discovery — no static signal databases
Same middleware from 100BASE-T1 to 10GBASE-T1
limitations: No hard real-time of its own — pair with TSN for deadlines
Heavier than signal-based CAN for tiny ECUs
real_world_example: An ADAS compute unit subscribing to a radar service's object-list events over 1000BASE-T1 SOME/IP.
frame_note: SOME/IP is serialized over UDP or TCP and (unlike SOME/IP-ET) can share one endpoint with several services by using distinct service IDs.

name: XCP (Universal Measurement & Calibration)
description: The calibration protocol: how engineers read thousands of internal ECU variables live and tweak maps while the engine runs — successor to CCP, transport-independent.
how_it_works: A master sends command packets (connect, get/set calibration page, program flash) while the ECU streams synchronous DAQ measurement lists at fixed raster rates — over CAN, FlexRay, Ethernet (XCPonEth) or USB.
speed: CAN: ~1000 signals @ 10 ms raster; Ethernet: 10k+ signals per raster
use_cases: ADAS logging at full bus load
advantages: One protocol for measurement AND flashing across all transports
Synchronous DAQ lists with timestamps — no polling jitter
limitations: Needs an A2L description file per ECU build or the addresses are meaningless
Seed-key security blocks casual access on production ECUs
real_world_example: Calibration tooling streaming 500 ECU signals at 1 ms raster over XCP-on-Ethernet during a dyno pull.
frame_note: XCP (Universal Measurement and Calibration Protocol) is XCP-on-CAN/Ethernet; the same packet framing supports both transports with a counter for ordering.

name: 10BASE-T1S (Single-Pair Ethernet)
description: Ethernet that finally speaks multidrop: 10 Mbps on ONE twisted pair with PLCA collision avoidance — positioned as the CAN/LIN successor for zonal edge nodes.
how_it_works: DME-coded differential signaling on a single pair; PLCA (Physical Layer Collision Avoidance) gives each node a transmit turn like a token, so a shared bus behaves deterministically without a switch.
advantages: Switched-Ethernet tooling (ping, TCP/IP, security) all the way to the edge sensor
One pair replaces CAN_H/CAN_L in new harnesses
limitations: 10 Mbps shared — one chatty node eats the bus; PLCA tuning required
Short reach (~25 m multidrop) vs RS-485 fieldbuses
real_world_example: A door-zone module hanging eight 10BASE-T1S sensors (latch, motor, puddle lamp) off one pair to the zonal gateway.
frame_note: T1S (Automotive Ethernet SerDes) signals on a single balanced pair with an embedded clock and pulse-width signalling instead of a separate clock lane.

name: UFS (Universal Flash Storage)
description: The managed-flash standard inside virtually every smartphone — SCSI-like command queueing over MIPI M-PHY serial lanes, soldered next to the SoC.
how_it_works: A UFS controller speaks SCSI commands (with command queueing and deep sleep states) over 1-2 UniPro/M-PHY differential lane pairs that scale gears from low-power PWM mode to HS-G5 bursts.
speed: HS-G4: 23.2 Gbps; UFS 4.0 (HS-G5): up to 46.4 Gbps
advantages: Full-duplex lanes + command queueing — far lower latency than eMMC
Deep hibernate states for battery life
limitations: BGA package + M-PHY tuning — not hobbyist-solderable
Overkill cost/complexity vs eMMC for slow embedded Linux
real_world_example: A flagship phone booting Android from a UFS 4.0 package at multi-GB/s sequential reads.
frame_note: UFS Transport Protocol (UTP) layers a 12-byte UFS header over each Logical Data Block; the digest protects data integrity.

technical.signaling: Device-to-device digital signaling; exact thresholds depend on the selected controller, peripheral, and I/O voltage.
technical.logic_high: Typically near the device I/O supply; confirm VOH/VIH in the device datasheet.
technical.logic_low: Typically near ground; confirm VOL/VIL in the device datasheet.
technical.voltage_reference: Common rails include 1.8 V, 3.3 V, and 5 V; do not mix incompatible domains.
technical.clocking: Synchronous, asynchronous, or encoded per the interface; check setup/hold and rise/fall limits.
technical.termination_and_biasing: Pull-ups, series resistors, and termination depend on the interface; follow its reference design.
design_notes: The protocol name alone does not set a voltage; the concrete device datasheet is authoritative.
technical.max_distance: Centimetres to ~1 m on PCB; use drivers/repeaters beyond that.
technical.max_nodes: 1 master + 1–8 slaves typical; bus variants allow up to 128 with addressing.
technical.duplex_mode: SPI full-duplex master/slave; I²C/UART half-duplex; check per interface.
technical.addressing: Chip-select, 7/10-bit address, or 64-bit ROM ID depending on the bus.
technical.error_detection: Parity / ACK-NACK / CRC-8/16 depending on the protocol layer.
technical.line_encoding: NRZ single-ended (CMOS/TTL) or open-drain; differential only via transceiver.
technical.power_profile: Logic supply 1.8–5 V; sleep µA to active mA — check MCU + peripheral datasheets.
technical.emc_isolation: Solid ground return, short stubs, series damping on fast edges; ESD array on connectors.

electrical.termination: On-die 100 Ohm termination; AC-coupled lanes
electrical.notes: Gen3 8 GT/s = 0.5 ns/bit (2 GT/s per lane, 128b/130b encoded). Gen4 doubles it with PAM4 at 16 GT/s. RX is clocked 2-3 UI later than TX - that skew is the whole design constraint.

name: NVMe
description: The protocol that retired AHCI: a streamlined, massively parallel SSD command set speaking directly over PCIe lanes with 64K queues of 64K commands each.
how_it_works: Host and SSD exchange doorbell-register plus submission/completion queue pairs in shared memory over PCIe — no legacy HDD emulation, MSI-X interrupts, optional fabrics (NVMe-oF) over Ethernet/RDMA.
speed: Gen3 x4: ~3.5 GB/s; Gen4 x4: ~7 GB/s; Gen5 x4: ~14 GB/s
use_cases: Edge-AI boxes logging GBs of sensor data
Boot media for compute modules (NVMe HATs)
advantages: Queue parallelism matches flash dies — far higher IOPS than SATA
Standard M.2/U.2 form factors across vendors
limitations: Needs PCIe lanes + NVMe driver stack — heavier than eMMC/SD
Active power and thermals need budgeting (heatsinks at Gen4+)
real_world_example: A single-board computer booting from an NVMe HAT at 800+ MB/s instead of 40 MB/s SD-card speeds.
fun_fact: NVMe 1.0 was published in 2011 after Intel concluded AHCI — designed for spinning disks — could never feed flash; a single NVMe queue pair already outperforms AHCI's entire single queue of 32 commands.
fun_fact_source: NVM Express 1.0 specification (2011); NVM Express workgroup history.
frame_note: NVMe queues admin and I/O commands as SQEs and returns CQEs; the 4-bit phase bit in the completion lets a poller tell new entries without a doorbell read.

technical.signaling: High-speed differential or encoded SERDES signaling implemented through transceiver/PHY hardware.
technical.logic_high: Not a universal logic-high voltage; receivers decode symbols or differential thresholds.
technical.logic_low: Not a universal logic-low voltage; receivers decode symbols or differential thresholds.
technical.voltage_reference: Voltage swing and common-mode are PHY/standard-specific; consult the transceiver design guide.
technical.clocking: Embedded, forwarded, or recovered clock; equalization and deskew may be required.
technical.termination_and_biasing: Controlled differential impedance, AC coupling, biasing, and termination are required.
design_notes: PCB stack-up, lane matching, reference clock, jitter, and channel loss are first-order constraints.
technical.max_distance: PCB traces: centimetres to ~50 cm; backplane/cable per loss budget (dB).
technical.max_nodes: Point-to-point lanes; fan-out via switch/retimer/redriver.
technical.duplex_mode: Full-duplex lane pairs (TX/RX); multi-lane bonding for throughput.
technical.addressing: Lane/endpoint enumeration per standard (e.g. PCIe BDF); no multi-drop addressing.
technical.error_detection: CRC + sequence numbers + link retraining / equalization handshake.
technical.line_encoding: 8b/10b, 64b/66b, 128b/130b scrambled NRZ or PAM-4 (per generation).

name: SATA (Serial ATA)
description: The ribbon-cable replacement that carried storage for two decades — 1.5/3/6 Gbps serial links with AHCI command sets, still everywhere in 2.5-inch SSDs and HDDs.
how_it_works: 8b/10b-encoded differential pairs carry FIS (Frame Information Structures) between host controller and device; AHCI exposes one command queue of 32; hot-plug and NCQ reorder requests for rotating media.
advantages: Cheap, hot-pluggable, enormous drive ecosystem
Simple cabling vs 40/80-wire PATA ribbons
limitations: AHCI single queue caps flash IOPS — NVMe is far faster
6 Gbps ceiling: a SATA SSD saturates at ~550 MB/s
real_world_example: A NAS box with four 6 Gbps SATA SSDs in RAID serving files at the gigabit-Ethernet limit.

frame_note: SATA uses fixed-size frames starting with a COMRESET SOF (FF F8 F8 FF) and a 32-bit CRC per dword, which is what makes hot-plug and error recovery reliable.

name: MAVLink
description: The drone world's lingua franca — a featherweight header-payload-checksum message set (HEARTBEAT, GLOBAL_POSITION, COMMAND_LONG) spoken by ArduPilot, PX4 and QGroundControl.
how_it_works: Fixed 0xFD magic, length/incompatibility/compatibility flags, 24-bit message ID and per-message CRC-extra seed; v2 signs packets for authenticated links and routes by system/component ID.
speed: Telemetry radios: 9.6–115.2 kbps; USB/Wi-Fi links: Mbps
frame_note: The magic byte distinguishes the dialect (0xFE = v2, 0xFD = v1), and MAVLink v2's 40-72 bit header adds incompatibility/compatibility flags plus a 48-bit message ID so two dialects can share a link and older parsers skip fields they do not know.
advantages: Tiny overhead, huge dialect ecosystem
Routing + packet signing built into v2
limitations: No security on v1 links — anyone with the frequency owns the drone
Dialect mismatches silently drop unknown messages
real_world_example: QGroundControl arming a PX4 quadcopter and streaming its GPS position over a 57600-baud telemetry radio.

technical.signaling: Aviation/aerospace signaling commonly uses differential, current-loop, or redundant wired links.
technical.logic_high: Not universally defined; use the approved transceiver and interface specification.
technical.logic_low: Not universally defined; use the approved transceiver and interface specification.
technical.voltage_reference: Aircraft buses may use 12/28 V power and specialized signal levels; do not infer them from bus names.
technical.clocking: Deterministic scheduling, redundancy, and fault containment are primary constraints.
technical.termination_and_biasing: Follow qualified wiring, termination, isolation, shielding, and redundancy requirements.
design_notes: Certification, radiation tolerance, and fault containment are part of the hardware design.
technical.max_distance: ARINC 429: 100+ m twisted/shielded; qualified harness per airframe.
technical.max_nodes: ARINC 429: 1 transmitter + up to 20 receivers; redundant channels per criticality.
technical.duplex_mode: Simplex (ARINC 429) or redundant dual-channel; higher layers add duplex.
technical.addressing: Label/SDI addressing plus system integration tables.
technical.error_detection: Parity + CRC + voter/monitor logic; redundancy management detects babbling units.
technical.line_encoding: Bipolar RZ (ARINC 429), Manchester/differential per avionics standard.
technical.power_profile: 28 V aircraft power via qualified converters; hold-up and lightning margins required.
technical.emc_isolation: Shielded/qualified wiring, lightning (DO-160) + HIRF protection, isolation barriers.

signals.name: VCC
signals.description: Supply for the transceiver, not the cable

electrical.termination: Series 33-100 Ohm with the logic ground; no terminator
electrical.notes: A bare UART is logic levels, not a standard: idle HIGH, start bit LOW, data LSB-first, then optional parity and stop bit(s). 9600 baud = 104 us/bit, but 10 bits per byte means 960 bytes/s. It has no clock line, which is why both ends must agree on the baud rate and why a wrong baud rate gives framing errors rather than garbage.

name: Cyphal (ex-UAVCAN)
description: A deterministic publish/subscribe + RPC middleware for robots and drones that runs on ordinary CAN FD buses — same wires as the ESCs, with DSDL-typed messages instead of raw frames.
how_it_works: Interfaces publish typed subjects and call RPC services; transports (CAN, UDP, serial) fragment DSDL-defined messages with transfer IDs, priorities and CRCs — the application never sees a raw CAN ID.
speed: CAN FD: up to 8 Mbps data phase; Cyphal/UDP: Ethernet rates
advantages: Plug-and-play node IDs + typed messages kill CAN-ID spreadsheets
Deterministic enough for flight control on cheap transceivers
limitations: Smaller ecosystem than ROS 2 for high-level autonomy
DSDL compile step unfamiliar to bare-metal teams
real_world_example: A VTOL's motor controllers publishing RPM setpoints as Cyphal subjects over one CAN FD bus.
frame_note: UAVCAN/Cyphal uses a 4-bit Transfer-ID that increments per session so a lost frame does not desynchronise the next request, plus a 7-bit node ID in the tail.

electrical.notes: A bare UART is logic levels, not a standard: idle HIGH, start bit LOW, data LSB-first, then optional parity and stop bit(s). 9600 baud = 104 us/bit, but 10 bits per byte means 960 bytes/s. It has no clock line, which is why both ends must agree on the baud rate and why a wrong baud rate gives framing errors rather than garbage.

name: TSN (Time-Sensitive Networking)
description: Not one protocol but a toolbox (Qbv time-aware shaper, Qbu preemption, gPTP sync) that turns ordinary Ethernet switches into deterministic, sub-microsecond-jitter fabric.
how_it_works: Bridges share a gPTP clock, then open/close egress gates on a repeating schedule (Qbv) so scheduled traffic can never queue behind a bulk transfer; preemption (Qbu) even splits a low-priority frame mid-flight.
speed: 100 Mbps – 10+ Gbps (profile of the underlying Ethernet)
use_cases: Converged factory networks (control + video + IT on one wire)
advantages: Determinism WITHOUT proprietary hardware — standard Ethernet silicon
One converged network replaces parallel control/IT cabling
limitations: Schedule engineering is genuinely hard (CNC tools required)
Both endpoints AND every switch must speak the same TSN profile
real_world_example: A car plant running robot control, camera inspection and office traffic on one TSN-switched network with guaranteed control latency.
frame_note: 802.1 TSN adds stream identity (Stream ID + Frame ID) so each talker/listener pair gets scheduled gates and reserved bandwidth.

electrical.termination: 100 Ohm (95 Ohm nominal) at both ends via a MagJack
electrical.notes: 10BASE-T at 10 Mbit/s is 100 ns/bit; 1000BASE-T is 1 ns/bit with 4D-PAM5 instead of Manchester. Manchester guarantees a transition every bit, which is why 10BASE-T needs no separate clock lane.

name: DDS (Data Distribution Service)
description: Brokerless pub/sub middleware with 20+ QoS policies (deadlines, durability, ownership) — the data bus inside ROS 2, ships, and surgical robots.
how_it_works: Typed topics flow over the RTPS wire protocol (usually UDP multicast) with discovery built in; QoS contracts are enforced per reader/writer pair, so a late sample is a contract violation, not silent lag.
speed: Bound by the transport (UDP/Ethernet); discovery chatter is the real budget
use_cases: Naval combat systems and air-traffic control
advantages: No broker means no single point of failure; discovery is automatic
QoS lets safety logic distinguish 'slow' from 'dead'
limitations: Multicast + discovery storms punish misconfigured VLANs
Heavier than MQTT for a lone temperature sensor
real_world_example: A warehouse robot fleet sharing pose topics over DDS with deadline QoS flagging any robot silent for over 100 ms.
frame_note: DDS-RTPS groups submessages by entity/topic in one multicast PDU, each preceded by a MessageId so partial delivery can be detected.

name: DMX512
description: Stage lighting's 512-channel workhorse: a continuously-repeated RS-485 universe where every dimmer just counts slots from the break — no addressing handshake at all.
how_it_works: The controller repeats: BREAK (line low 88+ us) + MAB + start code, then up to 512 channel bytes at 250 kbps 8N2; each fixture grabs its slot(s) by position and ignores the rest.
frame_note: Break/MAB are timed line conditions, not clocked bits — like I2C START/STOP they occupy no data bit. 8N2 framing (two stop bits) is mandatory.
advantages: Dead simple receivers — a tiny MCU can drive 512 channels
Deterministic ~23 ms refresh of the whole universe
limitations: No feedback, no error detection — a cut cable fails silently dark
One universe is 512 channels; big rigs need many universes via gateways
real_world_example: A theatre console fading 200 dimmers and 30 movers over one daisy-chained XLR run, refreshed 44 times a second.
fun_fact: DMX512's 250 kbps rate was chosen in 1986 because it was the fastest speed the cheap UARTs of the era could reliably manage — and the 44 Hz full-universe refresh it yields is still fast enough that audiences never see a step.
fun_fact_source: USITT DMX512/1986; ANSI E1.11-2008 (electrical/timing clauses).

name: KNX
description: The wired smart-building standard of Europe: sensors and actuators share a 29 V-powered twisted pair where every device is engineered (ETS) with group addresses instead of code.
how_it_works: Telegrams (control + routing + group address + up to 14-byte payload) travel TP1 lines at 9600 bps, coupled through line/area couplers into a building-wide tree; RF and IP tunneling extend it wirelessly and across floors.
speed: 9600 bps (TP1); 16–100 kbps (RF); IP backbone at Ethernet rates
advantages: Decentralized — no controller means no single point of failure
Decades of interoperable certified devices
limitations: ETS engineering software + certification cost for commercial jobs
9600 bps TP feels slow next to BACnet/IP
real_world_example: A hotel where the keycard, thermostat, blinds and bathroom light are four KNX devices sharing one bus with no central PC.
frame_note: KNX TP1 uses 8-bit telegrams (4-bit control, 4-bit length, 4-bit payload) or the extended 16-bit format; the checksum is even parity plus 0xFF padding.

name: DALI / DALI-2
description: Lighting control distilled: a 1200-bps, polarity-free 2-wire bus where every ballast has a short address, groups, and scenes — and DALI-2 adds sensors, buttons and certification.
how_it_works: Manchester-coded forward frames (16/24-bit: address + opcode) dim or query gear; gear answers with 8-bit backward frames; broadcast, group (16) and scene (16) commands address fixtures without reprogramming.
advantages: Polarity-free wiring installers cannot get wrong
Individual fixture feedback (lamp failure, power) unlike DMX
limitations: 64 addresses per bus — big floors need many buses/gateways
1200 bps: fades are stepped, not video-smooth
real_world_example: An office tower dimming 2000 DALI-2 luminaires by daylight sensor, each reporting its own lamp failures.
frame_note: DALI-2 sends a 16-bit forward frame and receives an 8-bit answer byte back-powering the line: only 1.2 kbit/s but 64 nodes and no separate return wire.

name: USB4
description: USB grows a router: 20–80 Gbps USB-C tunnels carrying USB3, DisplayPort and PCIe simultaneously, with bandwidth dynamically shared instead of fixed lanes.
how_it_works: A USB4 router discovers adapters at each end and tunnels USB3, DP and PCIe packets over 10/20 Gbps lanes; link training bonds lanes and reallocates bandwidth as displays and SSDs come and go.
advantages: One cable truly does everything — with dynamic, not wasted, bandwidth
Backward compatible to USB 2.0 electrically
limitations: Active cables + retimers mandatory at 40G+; cable quality matters enormously
Host/device certification matrix is genuinely confusing
real_world_example: A laptop driving two 4K monitors plus a fast SSD through one USB4 dock cable.
frame_note: USB4 tunnels PCIe, DisplayPort and USB3 traffic over 20+ Gbit/s using 64-byte Line Coding Blocks with a per-block CRC32 digest.

technical.signaling: Universal Serial Bus uses differential data pairs and separate control/clock signaling in newer generations.
technical.logic_high: USB data is encoded differential signaling; D+/D− are not a simple fixed logic-high rail.
technical.logic_low: USB data is encoded differential signaling; D+/D− are not a simple fixed logic-low rail.
technical.voltage_reference: USB 1.1/2.0 use 3.3 V transceiver signaling; USB 3.x adds high-speed differential lanes.
technical.clocking: Clock recovery is standard; USB 3.x adds separate high-speed transmit/receive lanes.
technical.termination_and_biasing: USB 2.0 uses a 1.5 kΩ pull-up; USB 3.x requires controlled differential impedance and AC coupling.
design_notes: Use a USB controller/PHY and follow connector, ESD, cable, and impedance requirements.
technical.max_distance: USB 2.0: 5 m; USB 3.x: 1–3 m passive (longer with active cable/retimer).
technical.max_nodes: 127 devices per host controller via hubs (shared bandwidth).
technical.duplex_mode: Half-duplex broadcast (USB 2.0); dual-simplex SuperSpeed pairs (USB 3.x).
technical.addressing: 7-bit device address assigned at enumeration; endpoint numbers per function.
technical.error_detection: CRC-5/CRC-16 on tokens/data + handshake retries (ACK/NAK/NYET/STALL).
technical.line_encoding: NRZI + bit stuffing (USB 2.0); 8b/10b or 128b/132b (USB 3.x).
technical.power_profile: 5 V VBUS: 100 mA (unconfigured) to 900 mA–5 A (BC/PD); negotiate before drawing.
technical.emc_isolation: 90 Ω diff routing, common-mode choke + ESD array, VBUS over-current protection.

electrical.termination: 90 Ohm differential per lane; lane rates up to 20 Gbit/s
electrical.notes: Up to 20 Gbit/s per lane (40 Gbit/s bidirectionally) using PAM4 at 40-80 GBd, which is why the swing shrinks to keep EMI down.

name: MIDI 1.0 / 2.0
description: Music's 31.25-kbps UART that outlived every computer port: note-on/off, velocity and control-change messages on an opto-isolated current loop — now joined by MIDI 2.0's 32-bit bidirectional property exchange.
how_it_works: MIDI 1.0 sends 1 status + 1-2 data bytes at 31.25 kbps over a 5 mA opto-isolated loop; running status omits repeats. MIDI 2.0 keeps the wire protocol and adds 32-bit UMP packets, profiles, and per-note control over USB/Ethernet transports.
advantages: Opto-isolation kills stage ground loops by design
Decades of compatible gear; files from 1983 still play
limitations: 7-bit velocity/resolution in 1.0 (steppy fades); 2.0 adoption still uneven
DIN daisy-chain latency adds ~1 ms per hop
real_world_example: A 1983 DX7 driving a modern laptop soft-synth through a USB-MIDI cable — unchanged wire protocol.
fun_fact: MIDI runs at the odd 31.25 kbps because in 1982 the only cheap crystal that divided down cleanly from synth master clocks gave exactly 1 MHz divided by 32 — the rate stuck so hard that MIDI 2.0 still honors it on DIN jacks.
fun_fact_source: MMA MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification (baud-rate clause); Dave Smith / Roland design history.
frame_note: MIDI runs on a 31.25 kbit/s current-loop DIN cable; most messages are 2-3 bytes with the first byte carrying message type and channel number in its nibbles.

technical.signaling: Digital audio/video signaling; CMOS, differential, encoded, or optical depending on the interface.
technical.logic_high: Usually near the interface supply for CMOS; differential/encoded interfaces use receiver thresholds.
technical.logic_low: Usually near ground for CMOS; differential/encoded interfaces use receiver thresholds.
technical.voltage_reference: Typical board signaling is 1.8 V or 3.3 V CMOS; professional differential/optical interfaces use their own standards.
technical.clocking: Usually synchronous with a bit clock, or clock-recovered from an encoded stream.
technical.termination_and_biasing: Use series damping, pull-ups/down, AC coupling, or 100 Ω differential termination as specified.
design_notes: Timing, impedance, and connector requirements are often more important than the label.
technical.max_distance: I²S/parallel: <10 cm on PCB; HDMI/DP: 2–15 m passive; SDI/optical: 100+ m.
technical.max_nodes: Point-to-point or source + sink; distribution via switch/splitter.
technical.duplex_mode: I²S full-duplex clocks + data; HDMI/DP unidirectional video + bidirectional control.
technical.addressing: Stream/channel select, device address, or EDID-negotiated endpoint.
technical.error_detection: Parity/channel-status (S/PDIF), ECC + CRC (HDMI/DP), retransmission on control channel.
technical.line_encoding: NRZ CMOS, biphase-mark (S/PDIF), TMDS / 8b/10b / 128b/132b (video links).
technical.power_profile: Codec 1.8/3.3 V; phantom power (mics) or 5 V (HDMI) per standard — never back-feed.
technical.emc_isolation: Continuous ground plane, 90/100 Ω diff routing, ESD on user-facing connectors.

electrical.termination: 220 Ohm to +5 V at the receiver, opto-isolated
electrical.notes: 31.25 kbit/s (32 us/bit) current loop at 5 mA. Active-low: a low pulses the opto LED on the receiver side.

name: IEEE 1394 (FireWire)
description: Apple's peer-to-peer serial bus that owned digital video in the 2000s — 400/800 Mbps, DMA straight into memory, devices that talk without any host computer.
how_it_works: Nodes arbitrate a shared cable tree with cycle-master isochronous slots (guaranteed 8 kHz video/audio bandwidth) plus async packets; 1394b adds 800 Mbps beta mode and longer runs.
use_cases: Industrial cameras and early portable players
advantages: True peer-to-peer + isochronous guarantees — no host needed
DMA speeds that embarrassed USB 2.0 (sustained, not burst)
limitations: Lost the connector war to USB (royalties + chipset politics)
DMA-from-any-device became a security concern for later buses
real_world_example: A 2000s editing suite capturing MiniDV tapes losslessly over a 6-pin FireWire 400 cable.
fun_fact: FireWire powered the first three iPod generations, and pro-audio FireWire interfaces were still being manufactured a decade after Apple removed the port — the 'FireWire is dead' headlines were premature.
fun_fact_source: IEEE 1394-1995 / 1394b-2002; Apple iPod technical specifications (2001–2004).
frame_note: IEEE 1394 (FireWire) uses asynchronous and isochronous packets distinguished by tcode, on a 100/400/800 Mbit/s daisy-chain with arbitration by node ID.

name: 6LoWPAN
description: The compression layer that finally put real IPv6 addresses on coin-cell 802.15.4 radios — the quiet foundation under Thread, Matter-over-Thread and most mesh sensor stacks.
how_it_works: IPv6/UDP headers (40+ bytes — bigger than a 127-byte 15.4 frame) are squeezed by LOWPAN_IPHC context compression, fragmented across frames, and mesh-routed to a border router speaking normal IPv6.
speed: 250 kbps PHY (802.15.4); ~100 kbps usable after mesh overhead
advantages: Every sensor gets a routable IPv6 address — no gateway translation hacks
Runs on the cheapest 15.4 silicon
limitations: Fragmentation punishes lossy links
Debugging compressed headers needs a 15.4 sniffer, not plain Wireshark
real_world_example: A utility's thousand-node meter mesh where each meter speaks IPv6 straight to the head-end system.
frame_note: This protocol has no fixed bit-level frame of its own: its data is carried by the physical/link layer below it, or it is a method inside a higher-layer message format. See the Electrical & Hardware Profile for the carrier that frames it.

technical.signaling: RF modulation; symbols are transmitted over the air rather than as fixed wire voltages.
technical.logic_high: No direct logic-high voltage; high-level state is represented by a modulation/symbol.
technical.logic_low: No direct logic-low voltage; low-level state is represented by a modulation/symbol.
technical.voltage_reference: Use radio frequency, transmit-power, antenna, and regulatory limits instead.
technical.clocking: PHY symbol timing and clock recovery depend on the radio generation.
technical.termination_and_biasing: RF matching, antenna impedance, and link budget replace wire termination.
design_notes: Document frequency, modulation, antenna interface, and regional power limits.
technical.max_distance: Link-budget dependent: metres (short-range) to kilometres (LoRa/cellular) line-of-sight.
technical.max_nodes: Star/mesh dependent; check gateway capacity and duty-cycle regulations.
technical.duplex_mode: Typically half-duplex TDD; full-duplex via paired bands or time slots on cellular.
technical.addressing: Network address (MAC/short address/IMSI); check join/provisioning procedure.
technical.error_detection: PHY CRC plus link-layer ARQ/FEC; see the Science Lab link-budget calculator.
technical.line_encoding: RF modulation (FSK, O-QPSK, OFDM, QAM, CSS); spreading/ FEC per standard.
technical.power_profile: Sleep current (µA) vs TX current (mA–A); duty cycle dominates battery life — budget with the link margin.
technical.emc_isolation: 50 Ω antenna match, keep-out zone, shielding; certify to regional radio regulations (ETSI/FCC).

electrical.termination: 50 Ohm antenna feed
electrical.notes: 250 kbit/s at 2.4 GHz (O-QPSK with 1/2-chip DSSS) - this is the physical half of both Zigbee and Thread.

name: NMEA 0183 / NMEA 2000 (GNSS & marine)
description: How position sensors talk: 0183's chatty comma-separated $GPGGA sentences at 4800 baud, and 2000's CAN-based PGN parameter groups — the GPS module on your desk speaks 0183.
how_it_works: 0183 talkers broadcast ASCII sentences (talker ID + comma fields + *checksum) that any number of listeners parse; 2000 replaces text with binary PGNs on a J1939-style 250 kbps CAN bus with standardized cabling.
advantages: 0183 is human-readable — debug with any serial terminal
2000 is plug-and-play multi-vendor on one backbone
limitations: 0183 has no addressing or error recovery — sentences just get lost
2000 certification + cabling costs vs plain serial GPS
real_world_example: A low-cost NEO-6M GPS module streaming $GPGGA sentences at 9600 baud into a tracker.
frame_note: NMEA 0183 sentences are ASCII terminated by CRLF with a single XOR checksum, so a sentence can be parsed by scanning for '$' then '*' without any framing bytes.

technical.signaling: Purpose-built sensor/actuator signaling, commonly a switched 24 V line, current loop, or synchronous sensor bus.
technical.logic_high: Use the sensor standard's high threshold; it may be voltage, current, or an encoded pulse.
technical.logic_low: Use the sensor standard's low threshold; it may be voltage, current, or an encoded pulse.
technical.voltage_reference: Industrial sensors commonly use 24 V DC, but signal levels and tolerances are interface-specific.
technical.clocking: May be edge-timed, current-modulated, or master-clocked; timing windows are part of the specification.
technical.termination_and_biasing: Use the specified pull-up/current path, load, shielding, and cable protection.
design_notes: Check parasitic power limits and inrush as well as data timing.
technical.max_distance: Metres (on-machine) to 100 m+ (current loop); check cable capacitance.
technical.max_nodes: Single sensor to multi-drop (e.g. IO-Link master with 8 ports).
technical.duplex_mode: Half-duplex interrogation; analog 4–20 mA is simplex continuous.
technical.addressing: Sensor address, channel number, or current-level signalling.
technical.error_detection: Checksum/CRC frame + out-of-range diagnostics; analog loops use live-zero (4 mA).
technical.line_encoding: Switched 24 V, 4–20 mA current loop, or synchronous serial per sensor bus.
technical.power_profile: 24 V industrial rail; M12 connector power classes; parasitic-power limits on 1-Wire.
technical.emc_isolation: Shielded cable, surge protection, separate analog/digital returns; IP-rated connectors.

signals.name: VCC
signals.description: Supply for the transceiver, not the cable

electrical.termination: Series 33-100 Ohm with the logic ground; no terminator
electrical.notes: A bare UART is logic levels, not a standard: idle HIGH, start bit LOW, data LSB-first, then optional parity and stop bit(s). 9600 baud = 104 us/bit, but 10 bits per byte means 960 bytes/s. It has no clock line, which is why both ends must agree on the baud rate and why a wrong baud rate gives framing errors rather than garbage.
